equipment_involved: Fluid Catalytic Cracking Unit (FCCU); Primary Absorber; Sponge Absorber; Gas Concentration Unit; Spent Catalyst Slide Valve; Asphalt Storage Tank 101
primary_failure_mode: Erosion of Spent Catalyst Slide Valve
root_cause_summary: The CSB determined that the explosion was caused by inadvertently directing air inside the regenerator through the reactor and main column into the gas concentration unit, where oxygen accumulated and formed a flammable mixture. This failure was the result of deficiencies in process knowledge regarding critical transient operation safeguards and reliance on a severely eroded spent catalyst slide valve.
regulatory_actions_mentioned: OSHA Citation and Notification of Penalty; EPA Consent Decree
qro_relevance_reasoning: The primary mechanical failure mode contributing to the disaster was severe erosion of the spent catalyst slide valve orifice and disc, which had experienced up to 85 percent metal loss in prior turnarounds and was normalized over 5-year operating cycles. Continuous, dynamic PoF modeling via QRO would have integrated historical inspection findings, operational differential pressure trends, and erosion degradation rates to flag the high Probability of Failure of the valve ahead of the turnaround. This would have alerted operators and reliability engineers that the valve could not function as a barrier, forcing corrective maintenance or enhanced transient operating safeguards prior to unit shutdown.

equipment_involved: 3-inch Cast Iron Y-Strainer; Isobutylene Charge Pump; Sulfurized Isobutylene Batch Reactor; Isobutylene Storage Tank and Piping
root_cause_summary: The CSB determined that the cause of the release was a brittle overload fracture of the cast iron y-strainer driven by internal pressure from liquid thermal expansion. KMCO's hazard evaluation programs consistently failed to identify that the y-strainer was constructed from brittle cast iron and installed in an isolated piping segment lacking pressure-relief protection.
regulatory_actions_mentioned: OSHA Process Safety Management Standard citations (29 CFR 1910.119); OSHA Emergency Action Plans citations (29 CFR 1910.38); OSHA HAZWOPER citations (29 CFR 1910.120); OSHA Employee Alarm Systems citations (29 CFR 1910.165); EPA Risk Management Program Rule (40 CFR Part 68)
qro_relevance_reasoning: QRO would have flagged this failure risk ahead of time by dynamically tracking historical maintenance data and component-level failure modes. The y-strainer previously developed a body crack and leaked in December 2015 due to thermal expansion pressure cycles, a critical warning sign that continuous probability of failure (PoF) modeling would have captured to trigger proactive replacement. Furthermore, evaluating brittle overload failure modes for cast iron components operating under cyclic hydro-static pressure in hazardous hydrocarbon service would have highlighted an unacceptable PoF score.

facility_name: Dow Louisiana Operations - Glycol II Plant
equipment_involved: Reflux Drum; Product Cooler; Rupture Disc; Emergency Pressure-Relief Valve; Reflux Pump; Pressure Relief Piping
primary_failure_mode: Foreign Debris Impact Rupture Disc Puncture
root_cause_summary: The CSB determined that the cause of the incident was the puncture of a rupture disc by metal debris that allowed the introduction of ethylene oxide into piping that contained air. Contributing to the incident was Dow's inadequate vessel closure procedures and practices, which allowed the vessel to be restarted without ensuring that it was adequately cleaned and the work lights removed.
regulatory_actions_mentioned: OSHA Process Safety Management (PSM) standard; EPA Risk Management Program (RMP) rule
qro_relevance_reasoning: Continuous process data modeling through QRO would have flagged the pressure transmitter readings in the pressure relief piping, which indicated atmospheric and negative gauge pressure (loss of nitrogen inerting) for over two years prior to the event. Furthermore, dynamically updating Probability of Failure models based on incoming reflux pump high-vibration interlock data would have alerted operations to circulating foreign object debris before the rupture disc was punctured.

equipment_involved: Amine Regeneration Unit (ARU7); Acid Gas Piping Flange; Sulfur Recovery Unit
primary_failure_mode: Inadvertent Opening of Active Equipment / Equipment Misidentification
root_cause_summary: The CSB determined that the cause of the incident was the opening of incorrect equipment, which released pressurized hydrogen sulfide gas. PEMEX Deer Park failed to establish an effective method to clearly identify the correct equipment to open before authorizing work and did not adequately evaluate the hazards posed to adjacent operating units.
regulatory_actions_mentioned: OSHA inspected PEMEX Deer Park and issued three citations with a proposed penalty of $49,650.
qro_relevance_reasoning: QRO software dynamically models Probability of Failure for physical mechanical asset degradation modes such as corrosion or fatigue based on inspection and operating history. This release was caused entirely by procedural human error and equipment misidentification when maintenance workers unbolted an active, pressurized acid gas line instead of an isolated one. Because the equipment did not fail due to material degradation, continuous risk modeling software would not have flagged or prevented this human-factor line-opening error.

equipment_involved: Hydrofluoric Acid Alkylation Unit; P14-B Depropanizer Reflux Pump Discharge Piping Elbow; V-1 Treater Feed Surge Drum; T-6 Depropanizer Distillation Column; T-7 Propane Stripper; V-11 Depropanizer Accumulator; HF Water Spray Mitigation System
root_cause_summary: The CSB determined the cause of the incident was the rupture of a steel piping component with high nickel and copper content that had corroded from HF and thinned faster than adjacent piping components with lower nickel and copper content. Contributing to the incident was the lack of requirements by the American Petroleum Institute, Sunoco, and PES, to inspect all existing carbon steel piping circuit components to ensure they could safely operate in HF service after the industry began quantifying the levels of nickel and copper in steel that could be considered safe for use in HF alkylation units in 2003.
regulatory_actions_mentioned: OSHA Process Safety Management (PSM) standard enforcement; EPA Risk Management Plan (RMP) rule revisions; EPA National Compliance Initiative on Reducing Risks of Accidental Releases; EPA Toxic Substances Control Act (TSCA) chemical prioritization
qro_relevance_reasoning: The incident was driven by accelerated hydrofluoric acid corrosion on an unmonitored carbon steel pipe elbow containing high residual nickel and copper content, which thinned down to 0.011 inches. QRO continuously models Probability of Failure at the component failure-mode level by incorporating material composition variations, localized damage mechanisms, and process operating conditions. By dynamically updating failure probabilities as new material degradation knowledge emerged, QRO would have flagged the uninspected elbow as a high-risk component requiring targeted inspection prior to rupture.

equipment_involved: Fuel Gas Mix Drum; Crude 1 Tower; Crude 1 Overhead Accumulator Drum; Coker Gas Plant Absorber Stripper Tower; Naphtha Hydrotreater Preheat Heat Exchangers
root_cause_summary: The CSB determined the cause of the incident was operators opening valves and removing a flange on the pressurized Fuel Gas Mix Drum to release flammable naphtha directly to the ground, creating a vapor cloud that ignited. Contributing factors included the refinery's failure to implement engineered safeguards against vessel overfill, severe alarm flooding, ineffective abnormal situation management, and an over-reliance on human intervention.
regulatory_actions_mentioned: OSHA Process Safety Management Standard; OSHA Hazard Alert Letter; OSHA Citations; EPA Risk Management Program Rule
qro_relevance_reasoning: This incident was driven by acute operational disturbances, process instability, extreme alarm flooding, and manual human intervention releasing liquid naphtha to the ground. Continuous quantitative PoF modeling at the failure-mode level focuses on equipment degradation and mechanical integrity, which would not predict or prevent real-time operational decision-making errors and overfill management failures occurring within hours.

equipment_involved: Heat Exchanger AW234; Graphite Vapor Outlet Nozzle; PTFE-lined Carbon Steel Piping
root_cause_summary: The CSB determined the cause of the incident was the inadvertent over-torquing of bolts on an HCl piping flange connection to a heat exchanger, which resulted in the fracture of the heat exchanger outlet piping and a release of gaseous HCl in the vicinity of seven contract workers. Wacker's lack of written procedures and lack of control of hazardous energy contributed to the occurrence of the event, while a lack of a SIMOPs program and limited means of egress contributed to its severity.
regulatory_actions_mentioned: OSHA Process Safety Management (PSM) Standard (29 CFR 1910.119); EPA Risk Management Program (RMP) Rule (40 CFR 68); Tennessee Occupational Safety and Health Administration (TOSHA)
qro_relevance_reasoning: QRO would not have flagged this failure ahead of time because the incident resulted from an instantaneous brittle overload caused by manual over-torquing of flange bolts during maintenance. Continuous PoF modeling is designed to track cumulative degradation mechanisms such as corrosion, cracking, or wall thinning rather than immediate human procedural errors during bolt torquing. Because there was no underlying material degradation prior to the over-torquing event, continuous data-driven risk modeling would not have predicted the release.

equipment_involved: Sulfuric Acid Alkylation Unit; Quarter-turn Plug Valve; Plug Valve Gearbox
root_cause_summary: The incident occurred due to poor equipment design that allowed gearbox support brackets to be mounted using pressure-retaining top-cap bolts, combined with a lack of human factors evaluations. Additionally, the facility lacked written procedures and worker training on safely removing inoperable gearboxes, relying on an informal practice of manual gearbox removal.
regulatory_actions_mentioned: OSHA Process Safety Management (PSM) Standard (29 C.F.R. § 1910.119)
qro_relevance_reasoning: The loss of containment was caused by an operator inadvertently unbolting a valve's pressure-retaining top-cap while removing a malfunctioning gearbox, rather than physical asset degradation or damage mechanisms. Continuous quantitative Probability of Failure (PoF) software models degradation failure modes over time, but cannot forecast human error or procedural missteps during field maintenance activities.
